{{recipesummary|category=Sauce recipes|servings=6|time=45 minutes|difficulty=2|Image=[[Image:Ravioli Marinara.jpg|300px]]}}
{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of Italy|Cuisine of Italy]] | [[Cookbook:Sauces|Sauces]]

'''Marinara''' (mariner's) sauce is a southern Italian [[cookbook:Tomato Sauce|tomato sauce]] usually made with tomatoes, garlic, herbs (such as basil), and onion.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marinara Definition & Meaning {{!}} YourDictionary |url=https://www.yourdictionary.com/marinara |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=www.yourdictionary.com}}</ref> However, there are many variations. Some of these include the addition of [[cookbook:caper|capers]], olives and spices.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Marinara Sauce |url=https://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/giada-de-laurentiis/marinara-sauce-recipe2-1950802 |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=Food Network |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=https://www.facebook.com/seriouseats |title=The Best Italian-American Tomato Sauce Recipe |url=https://www.seriouseats.com/the-best-slow-cooked-italian-american-tomato-sauce-red-sauce-recipe |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=Serious Eats |language=en}}</ref>

There are at least two folk theories as to the origin of this sauce: One says cooks aboard Neapolitan ships invented marinara sauce in the mid-16th century after Spaniards introduced the [[cookbook:tomato|tomato]] (a New World vegetable) to Europe. This meat-free sauce was easy to make and resisted spoiling due to the high acid content of tomatoes. This made it ideal for lengthy sea voyages hundreds of years before refrigeration methods were invented. Another theory states this was a sauce prepared by the wives of Neapolitan sailors upon their return from sea. Historically, however, we know the first Italian cookbook to include tomato sauce,<ref>Elizabeth David, ''Italian Food'' (1954, 1999), p 319, and John Dickie, ''Delizia! The Epic History of the Italians and Their Food'', 2008, p. 162.</ref> ''Lo Scalo alla Moderna'' (''The Modern Steward''), was written by Italian chef Antonio Latini and was published in two volumes in 1692 and 1694. Latini served as the Steward of the First Minister to the Spanish Viceroy of Naples.<ref>Alan Davidson, "Europeans' Wary Encounter with Tomatoes, Potatoes, and Other New World Foods" in ''Chilies to Chocolate: Food the Americas Gave the World'', (University of Arizona Press) 1992.</ref><ref>Elizabeth David, ''Italian Food'' (1954, 1999), p 319, and John Dickie, ''Delizia! The Epic History of the Italians and Their Food'', 2008, p. 162.</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The Food Timeline history notes--sauce |url=https://www.foodtimeline.org/foodsauces.html |access-date=2023-06-27 |website=www.foodtimeline.org}}</ref>

Traditional southern Italian cuisine utilizes this sauce to add flavor to pasta, rice, seafood and pizza. This sauce is also widely used in [[cookbook:Italian-American cuisine|Italian-American cuisine]] which has diverged significantly from its Old World origins. Italians refer to marinara only in association with other recipes. For instance, ''spaghetti alla marinara'' literally translates to '''mariner's spaghetti'''. However, tomato sauce alone in Italy is called ''salsa al pomodoro'' or ''pummarola''.

The recipe below is based on the one by world-renowned chef Mario Batali cited in the references section below.

== Ingredients ==
*6 [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoons]] virgin [[cookbook:olive oil|olive oil]]
*225 [[Cookbook:Gram|grams]] (8 [[Cookbook:Ounce|ounces]]) Spanish [[cookbook:onion|onion]], [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]]
*4 cloves [[cookbook:garlic|garlic]], thinly [[Cookbook:Slicing|sliced]]
*2 [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoons]] fresh [[cookbook:thyme|thyme]] leaves (or ½ teaspoon dried)
*4 teaspoons fresh [[cookbook:basil|basil]] leaves (or 1 teaspoon dried)
*85 grams (3 ounces) red [[Cookbook:Bell Pepper|bell pepper]], diced
*1.3 [[Cookbook:Kilogram|kilograms]] (1 [[Cookbook:Pound|pound]] and 14 ounces) skinless plum [[cookbook:tomato|tomatoes]], crushed by hand
*1 tablespoon [[Cookbook:Sugar|sugar]]
*[[Cookbook:Salt|Salt]] to taste

== Preparation ==
#Heat the oil in a [[Cookbook:Saucepan|saucepan]] over medium heat until it shimmers.
#Add the onions and garlic, and [[cookbook:saute|sauté]] them for about 2 minutes until the onions are translucent.
#Add the thyme, basil and bell pepper. Cook 5 minutes more.
#Add the tomatoes and sugar. Bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]] and then lower to a light [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]], stirring occasionally for 30 minutes.
#Season with salt to taste.
#Serve hot by ladling over pasta, seafood or rice.
